newsitem.title: NEW ZEALAND: NZ's Brierley says healthy despite profit fall.
newsitem.headline: NZ's Brierley says healthy despite profit fall.

text.p: New Zealand's Brierley Investments Ltd on Thursday declared itself in excellent health despite a 32 percent drop in first half profit, saying its investment focus on Australasia was paying off and prescribing more of the same.

BIL reported an interim profit of NZ$116 million (US$81.4 million), down from NZ$170 million a year earlier, but said its listed investments were valued by the market at more than NZ$500 million above book values.
"Our key focus is on increasing the value of the company's underlying assets. In this context we are well pleased with our achievements to date," Chairman Bob Matthew told a briefing.
The market agreed, BIL's share price remaining steady at NZ$1.36 after the profit was announced.

"A single lower profit doesn't really matter. Profit is going to be lumpy with an investment company depending on what they sell and when the gains come through," said Guy Hallwright, analyst at First NZ Capital.
"Over time they need to be higher than this, but you are going to get these timing issues which will produce some low and some very high results."
Lower trading contributions from investments over the period depressed the profit.

Air New Zealand, in which BIL has a 42 percent stake, contributed about NZ$25 million less at the half year, while 100 percent owned Australian retailer Vox had incurred a loss of A$13.9 million (US$10.9 million).
Chief Executive Paul Collins said the highlight of the year had been the successful flotation of Britain's Thistle Hotels.

This had achieved BIL's objective of reducing its investment in Thistle -- from 70 percent to 46 percent -- while at the same time retaining a strategic stake in a profitable company with solid growth prospects.
But Australasia remains BIL's focus.

Collins said the company had doubled its exposure to New Zealand and Australia over the last four and a half years, with 60 percent of assets, about NZ$3.5 billion, invested in New Zealand and Australia at December 1996.

"The real issue for us in Australasia is we don't have any competition. We don't actually have competition at all in New Zealand for the size of investment we go into, and we don't have competition in Australia," Collins said.
"So we do get the opportunity to look at a wide range of those sorts of investments."

BIL's exposure in Australia had risen substantially from NZ$678 million at June 1996 to NZ$1.25 billion at December 31, due mainly to the acquisition of a 20 percent stake in publisher John Fairfax for NZ$503 million.
Collins said the market value of BIL's Fairfax stake was already around NZ$544 million.
"It is one of the world's top publishing assets," he said, adding that BIL saw very positive prospects for Fairfax and had invested for the long haul.
BIL's interest in Asia was also growing, with an increased investment in public companies of just over NZ$100 million.

"That's primarily new listed stocks which we're looking at, mostly out of Hong Kong but a small amount out of other parts of Asia as well. None of those are actually in stakes which are at disclosable levels at the present time," Collins said.
Analysts said that unless BIL makes a significant asset sale this financial year, its full year profit will come in lower than the NZ$310 million 1995/96 result.
Collins declined to comment on the company's plans for future asset sales, saying only that the full year result would be "acceptable".
